chunks: First: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fudalah from Aban from Sulayman ibn Abdillah al-Hashimi from his father, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who bequeathed to a man, and he gave him one thousand dirhams as the zakat of his wealth, and it was lost by the executor. He said: He is liable (guarantor) and he does not return it to the heirs.
Second: From him (Al-Husayn) from Fudalah from Aban from a man, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who bequeathed to a man that there is a debt upon him. He said: The man pays what is upon him of his debt and divides what remains among the heirs. I said: If what was bequeathed from the debt was stolen, from whom is the debt taken? From the heirs or from the executor? He said: It is not taken from the heirs, but the executor is liable for it.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The meaning in these two narrations is that the executor is only liable for the wealth if he was able to deliver it to its rightful owner, but did not, and it was lost. As for if he was not able to do so, and then it was lost without negligence on his part, there is nothing upon him.
Third: What Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him):

He said about a man who died and bequeathed to a man, and the deceased had a debt. The one bequeathed to went and set aside the debt for the creditors, raised it in his house, and divided what remained among the heirs. If what was for the creditors was stolen at night, from whom is it taken? He said: He is liable when he set it aside in his house; it is paid from his wealth.
ai.seo_question: Is the executor liable if the bequeathed wealth is lost or stolen?
ai.summary: These narrations from al-Isfabar establish the executor (al-wasi) as a trustee (dhimma) whose liability for lost bequeathed wealth depends on whether the loss resulted from his negligence or unavoidable circumstances. The juristic analysis by Muhammad ibn al-Hasan clarifies that liability attaches only when the executor had the capacity to deliver the assets but failed to do so, distinguishing between mere loss and culpable delay. This principle underscores the fiduciary responsibility of the executor in settling the deceased's debts and distributing the remainder to heirs.
